summary: Redwood-led security deep-dive focusing on Private/VPC and on-prem deployment patterns. topics: VPC/subnet topology; ingress egress and NAT; firewall rules and IDS; bastion vs private link; on-prem connector (air-gap considerations); KMS/HSM integration and key rotation; SAML/SCIM/SSO; audit logs and SIEM forwarding; retention & data residency
transcript:
[00:00] Evan Brooks: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're going to run through the VPC and on-prem security architecture for PulseHealth. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Laura Chen: Laura here, CISO.
[00:10] Miguel Rivera: Miguel, head of infra.
[00:12] Priya Shah: Priya, platform eng.
[00:14] Tom Alvarez: Tom, security ops.
[00:16] Rina Luo: Rina from Redwood, solutions eng.
[00:20] Evan Brooks: Great. Goal for today is to validate network isolation, ingress/egress patterns, firewalling and how our Private offering would sit in your VPC or on-prem. Also cover KMS and logging.
[00:30] Laura Chen: High-level — our bar is SOC 2 and ISO27001 alignment. We also need full auditability and SSO. We'll probably want an HSM option for key control.
[00:43] Rina Luo: Totally, and that's in scope. Two deployment patterns we typically see: 1) Redwood Private running in a customer VPC (we run the control plane in your VPC or with a private peering) and 2) on-prem package for air-gapped sites. For VPC we can use private subnets plus a managed NAT/egress path. For on-prem we support an on-prem connector that does outbound-only TLS to a control endpoint if required.
[01:10] Miguel Rivera: When you say outbound-only, do you mean we open a single egress port and everything else blocked? We need to understand IPs, ports, and how to firewall tightly.
[01:22] Rina Luo: Yes. We try to minimize inbound holes. For the managed on-prem connector the recommended pattern is an egress-only firewall rule to allow TLS (443) to a small set of Redwood IPs or hostnames; we give an allowlist window for maintenance. If you need stricter controls we also support a broker/proxy pattern so traffic flows through your proxy.
[01:40] Tom Alvarez: And what about mutual TLS or client certs? We prefer mTLS for critical traffic.
[01:46] Evan Brooks: We support mTLS for the connector and also can do IP-based allowlisting. For Private inside the VPC we can either run in your account so you control the security groups and subnets, or we can place instances in a dedicated account with VPC peering. Both are options depending on compliance needs.
[02:04] Priya Shah: If you run in our account, who manages the Bastion and jump hosts? Our infra team wants to manage bastions and deny direct internet to nodes.
[02:12] Rina Luo: In the customer-managed account pattern, you manage bastions and KMS. Redwood provides AMIs/images and orchestration manifests. For fully managed we can provide a hardened bastion as part of the offering but we can also disable it if you prefer.
[02:28] Miguel Rivera: Can you outline the recommended subnet layout — I need to show the firewall team.
[02:33] Rina Luo: Sure — we usually recommend: public subnet for a small NAT/egress appliance if needed, private subnets for inference nodes (no inbound internet), and a management subnet for control plane components. Control-plane endpoints are either internal-only or exposed through private link. We can annotate with route tables showing default route to NAT gateway for egress.
[02:54] Evan Brooks: I'll share a diagram after the call; Rina will produce an annotated VPC sketch.
[02:58] Laura Chen: Logging — we need audit logs forwarded to our Splunk instance. Timestamps, user IDs, actions, and API arguments. What's the retention and the format?
[03:10] Rina Luo: We emit structured audit events. For Private deployments we can forward logs to your S3 bucket or a syslog/Splunk forwarder. We support JSON events with fields for user, token id, request path, and result. Retention is controlled by you if logs go to your storage; otherwise Redwood can retain per contract.
[03:30] Tom Alvarez: How do we guarantee logs are tamper-evident? We need a chain-of-custody.
[03:36] Evan Brooks: Two patterns: forward to your SIEM in near-real-time, or we can push signed log bundles with a hash chain. For the highest assurance, use your HSM-backed KMS to sign events — that's available in the on-prem pattern.
[03:52] Priya Shah: Key management — we want control of keys. Can we bring our own KMS keys?
[03:58] Rina Luo: Yes, BYOK is supported. On cloud we integrate with AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault; for on-prem we can integrate with HSMs via PKCS#11 or via a gateway. We support key rotation policies and can store model-encryption keys encrypted under your KMS.
[04:16] Miguel Rivera: Do you ever store plaintext model or data on Redwood side?
[04:19] Evan Brooks: No, for Private deployments the data paths are inside your network; in hosted we have zero plaintext retention unless contracted. For extra assurance we can enable envelope encryption so that any artifact saved is encrypted by customer KMS.
[04:34] Laura Chen: SSO and RBAC — we use Okta and SCIM. Can you provision roles and sync groups?
[04:40] Rina Luo: Absolutely. We support SAML SSO and SCIM for group provisioning. Roles in the console map to RBAC roles and can be scoped to environments and projects. We also maintain an audit trail of role changes.
[04:55] Tom Alvarez: Network IDS/IPS — how do you support host-level detection? Do you provide EDR agents?
[05:01] Rina Luo: We don't currently ship EDR, customers typically run their own EDR on nodes. We can output host and app-level telemetry to your collector. For network IDS we can mirror traffic to your NIDS from a tap or use VPC Flow Logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[05:17] Miguel Rivera: What about ingress? We have strict rules — only services that need to receive traffic should be exposed, and only via ALB with WAF.
[05:24] Evan Brooks: Our recommendation is ALB + WAF in front of any public endpoints and then private subnets for inference. For model serving endpoints that must be reachable from your app, use internal ALB and private link. We avoid exposing any admin plane publicly.
[05:40] Priya Shah: Can you lock down metadata endpoints and IMDS?
[05:42] Rina Luo: Yes — best practice is to enforce IMDSv2 and restrict Instance Role permissions. We'll provide guidance for hardening OS and container runtime.
[05:52] Laura Chen: Air-gapped sites — we have one facility that is semi-airgapped. How would Redwood operate in that environment?
[05:58] Rina Luo: For air-gapped we offer an on-prem bundle: it's essentially a self-contained package that doesn't require outbound connectivity. Deployment includes a local registry, local model artifacts, and an on-prem control plane. Updates are delivered via signed bundles you pull through an operator. This is heavier and requires a different support SLA.
[06:16] Miguel Rivera: For the semi-airgapped site we could allow a periodic maintenance window for outbound sync — would that work?
[06:20] Evan Brooks: Yes, a sync window for updates and metrics push is common. During that window you can open a narrow egress window to Redwood's update endpoints. We'll provide signed artifacts and checksums.
[06:31] Tom Alvarez: Firewalling specifics — we need port lists. Are you able to provide IPs for allowlisting?
[06:36] Rina Luo: We can provide an allowlist CIDR range and also granular FQDNs. For fully-private deployments running in-customer-account there may be no external IPs to allowlist — everything stays internal. For connector patterns, we'll supply IP ranges and expected ports (443, 9411 for tracing if enabled, 5222 for internal control if using legacy protocol — note: that's a legacy example and may not be enabled).
[07:00] Laura Chen: Can the control plane be put behind PrivateLink/VPCE?
[07:04] Rina Luo: Yes, we support PrivateLink and endpoint services. That is a common enterprise deployment to avoid public endpoints.
[07:12] Priya Shah: How about multi-tenant isolation — if we run dedicated capacity in our VPC but host multiple teams, are there tenant boundaries?
[07:19] Evan Brooks: We support tenant isolation via namespaces and network policies. For strict isolation you can carve out separate subnets or VPCs per tenant. We can also enforce per-tenant KMS keys.
[07:33] Miguel Rivera: Let's talk about egress filtering for model artifacts — outbound model pull from public repos is a risk. Can we forbid outbound to arbitrary ecr/docker hub?
[07:41] Rina Luo: Yes — we can stage model artifacts in your private registry. In on-prem or VPC patterns, we recommend mirroring models to your repo. The orchestration can be configured to only pull from allowed registries.
[07:54] Tom Alvarez: Auditability — who has access to console actions? We need granular audit logs including who invoked a model and token-level context.
[08:02] Rina Luo: We capture API-level audit logs with user/timestamp/action. Token-level tracing is possible but we redact sensitive prompt content by default; you can opt-in to enhanced logging during tests. All logs can be forwarded to your SIEM or stored in your S3 with lifecycle policies.
[08:19] Laura Chen: Pen tests and certs — can you share recent pentest summaries and SOC2 report?
[08:24] Evan Brooks: Yes — I'll attach the redacted pen test summary and SOC2 attestation after this call. We'll also include control mappings for how our Private offering maps to your requirements.
[08:36] Priya Shah: Network policy enforcement for containers — we use CNI policies (Calico). Does Redwood support Calico network policies?
[08:43] Rina Luo: Yes. Our runtime can respect whatever CNI enforcement you have. We ship the necessary hooks to honor Kubernetes network policies.
[08:50] Miguel Rivera: What about egress to telemetry endpoints — we need assurances that telemetry can't exfiltrate model artifacts or PII.
[08:58] Rina Luo: Telemetry is limited to operational metrics and anonymized stats by default. For Private deployments you can disable telemetry or forward it to a sink you control. Exfiltration controls include egress filtering and content scanning before any outgoing telemetry.
[09:14] Tom Alvarez: For KMS rotation — how do you handle key rotation without downtime?
[09:19] Evan Brooks: We use envelope encryption: data keys are rewrapped with the new KMS key and rotation can be done online. We recommend a rolling rewrap window and we provide tooling to automate that. If using customer-managed KMS, rotation is coordinated with you.
[09:34] Laura Chen: Are there any known gotchas with SCTP or UDP for model serving? We rely on TCP generally.
[09:39] Rina Luo: Our serving stack uses TCP/TLS for token streams; we don't require SCTP/UDP. If you have UDP-only network devices, that's outside scope.
[09:46] Evan Brooks: Quick recap — we'll send diagrams, IP/port allow list, SOC2 docs, and schedule the bench test. Any other blockers?
[09:53] Miguel Rivera: We need the allowlist and a list of operations that require outbound vs inbound. Also SLA on on-prem offerings — response times for air-gapped incidents.
[10:03] Evan Brooks: We'll include a proposed SLA in the package; on-prem air-gap does have a slightly different SLA.
[10:10] Priya Shah: One last item — how do you handle patching for on-prem nodes?
[10:13] Rina Luo: For on-prem we provide patch bundles and guidance; for customer-managed nodes you apply patches. For fully-managed nodes in your account Redwood can apply OS and runtime patches per a maintenance window.
[10:24] Laura Chen: Ok good. Please include a clear diagram showing subnets, bastion, NAT, endpoint type (private link vs public), and where KMS sits.
[10:33] Evan Brooks: Noted. Rina will follow up with the diagram and we'll get the bench on the calendar. Thanks everyone.
[10:40] Tom Alvarez: Thanks, good session.
[10:42] (call ends)
